vignette:
Maya

Maya sits in the waiting room of the university library where she works, her fingers tracing the edge of her laptop bag. She's twenty years old, with an easy smile that doesn't quite reach her eyes anymore. She works as an auditor for the university's financial compliance department-a job she was genuinely excited about when she started it two years ago. The work suited her: methodical, detail-oriented, the kind of job where you could lose yourself in numbers and patterns.

It started eight months ago, though Maya didn't realize it was starting. A man she'd met at a campus event kept appearing places. At first, she thought it was coincidence. Then he began messaging her through multiple accounts after she'd blocked the first one. The messages weren't always threatening, which somehow made it worse-they were intimate, presumptive, as if they shared something they didn't. He knew things about her schedule, her routines. He knew when she went to the gym. He knew which coffee shop she visited on Thursday mornings.

The police took a report. Nothing illegal enough, they said. Not yet. The word yet has lived in Maya's chest ever since.

Now, eight months later, Maya moves through her days like someone navigating a room in the dark. She's hyperaware of exits. When she's at her desk in the audit office, she positions herself so she can see the door. She's changed her routes to work three times, and she still doesn't feel safe. Every notification on her phone sends her heart rate spiking-a reflexive jolt before she even looks at who's messaging her. She's deleted most of her social media accounts. The ones she keeps, she doesn't post on. No locations, no schedules, nothing that could be used as a map of her life.

Sleep is fragmented. She lies awake in her apartment, listening to sounds in the hallway. Sometimes she's convinced she hears him. Other times, she's convinced she should be hearing him, that her vigilance is the only thing keeping something terrible from happening. When she does sleep, she has dreams where she's being followed through endless corridors, her legs moving in slow motion while footsteps get closer.

At work, she's become someone else. Her supervisor has noticed. Maya used to be engaged in her audits, asking questions, suggesting improvements. Now she does her work competently but mechanically, speaking only when necessary. She eats lunch at her desk instead of going out. She's declined invitations to after-work drinks. She can't explain to her colleagues why she flinches when someone approaches her desk from behind, or why she sometimes excuses herself to the bathroom and doesn't return for twenty minutes.

The worst part is the uncertainty. The man hasn't done anything in three months. No messages, no sightings. But Maya can't relax into the silence. Instead, it feels like waiting. It feels like the calm before something. She oscillates between hypervigilance and a strange numbness-moments where she feels disconnected from her own body, watching herself go through the motions of being a normal twenty-year-old who works as an auditor and has a life that makes sense.

She knows intellectually that she's not responsible for what he did. But her body doesn't believe that. Her body believes she's in danger. Her body is always, always preparing for the next threat.
